Yet, allowing profits to be uncapped creates potential system-wide stability risks, as extreme profits could trigger excessive market volatility. This study examines how limiting maximum profits influences market prices within these settings. Specifically, this research analyzes a static game featuring an electric utility company and a competitive retail sector. The utility provides power over a specific duration with demand determined by a static inverse demand curve, established within a framework of unsteady (volatile) states. The game involves strategic choices regarding generation levels and prices (which can either face regulatory caps or operate without limits on profits). The analysis focuses on two scenarios: an environment regulated by price ceilings and an environment without such regulatory limits. Comparative statics methods are employed to examine equilibrium outcomes across both the regulated and unregulated models. The findings indicate that removing profit regulations tends to lower consumer surplus within the competitive sales environment; however, this effect is conditional and operates within specific parameter ranges to avoid local complexity. Under the regulated model, the strategic decision point (kink location) exhibits stability against market demand fluctuations, ensuring robust model behavior. Conversely, in the absence of profit caps, this decision point remains vulnerable to extreme demand surges, highlighting a lack of robustness. When profits are unregulated but the sales competition remains highly aggressive, an equilibrium may fail to exist entirely. Introducing regulated profits stabilizes these fragile equilibria, though this restoration also occurs in non-regulated scenarios only under circumstances of limited market aggression.
